before: A condition treats a value as truthy or falsy. That is different from checking whether the value is missing.
false, 0, an empty string, null, undefined, and NaN are falsy. Empty arrays and empty objects are truthy.
Choose the default rule from the requirement. A user’s zero volume or false notification setting may be intentional, not missing.
Neither operator validates a value’s type. Preserving false is correct for this exercise; a different contract may reject it.
after: A condition treats values as truthy or falsy: as a yes or a no. That is different from asking whether a setting is missing.
Values such as `false`, `0`, `""`, `null`, `undefined`, and `NaN` are falsy. Empty arrays and empty objects are truthy.

`||` uses the right value when the left one is falsy:
```javascript
console.log(0 || 10);
console.log("" || "Guest");
```
Output:
```text
10
Guest
```

`??` uses the right value only when the left one is `null` or `undefined`:
```javascript
console.log(0 ?? 10);
console.log(false ?? true);
```
Output:
```text
0
false
```
Choose the rule the setting needs. Zero volume and notifications set to false can be deliberate choices. Do not replace them just because they are falsy.
These operators choose a value; they do not check whether its type is allowed. This exercise keeps every supplied value except `null` and `undefined`.
